header:
Date: 2027-08-03 16:00 PDT
Duration: 38 minutes
Location: Zoom (recording)
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Evan (Redwood SE), Maya (Redwood Marketing), Jordan (Producer); Dr. Anika Rao (Peregrine CTO), Liam O'Connor (Head of Product), Jules Moreno (Eng Lead), Priya Menon (Data Scientist)
summary: Podcast-style customer interview capturing Peregrine Biotech's journey moving an internal research assistant from a prototype on consumer LLM endpoints to a production inference pipeline on Redwood Dedicated. Conversation covers performance wins, cost trade-offs, security/KMS considerations, and measurable business impact. Agreed next steps: produce marketing assets, share security docs and benchmarks, and finalize a co-branded case study.
topics: cost per inference and batching/caching optimizations
workflow: dev->staging->prod rollout with Redwood Dedicated
marketing use: customer quotes and highlight reels
questions: What were the key criteria that made you choose Redwood over other providers?
How did you validate latency and throughput in your POC?
What privacy or compliance controls were non-negotiable for you?
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Host): Welcome everyone, this is the Redwood customer spotlight with Peregrine Biotech, thanks for joining. Quick audio check?
[00:08] Dr. Anika Rao: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks for having us.
[00:12] Sofia (AE): Hi team, really excited for this chat. Hey Liam, Jules - thanks for making time.
[00:18] Liam: Happy to be here.
[00:20] Jordan (Producer): Recording started.
[00:24] Maya: Great, so the format — we'll do about 30 minutes of conversation, then a few quick lightning questions. Start with a bit of background: Anika, can you describe the product you were trying to put into production?
[00:36] Dr. Anika: Sure, so at Peregrine we build a research assistant for bench scientists. It's, uh, a tool that ingests experimental notes, protocols, and returns suggested next steps and relevant literature. The prototype used off-the-shelf consumer endpoints and, uh, it worked fine for early trials but we hit limits when we tried to scale to real lab usage.
[00:57] Liam: To add, latency was variable and costs spiked when a few teams ran long chains of prompts. We wanted predictability and an ops story.
[01:10] Sofia: And that's where you engaged Redwood initially for a POC, correct? Can you walk us through that?
[01:16] Jules: Yes — we did a two-week POC. Redwood helped us spin up Dedicated capacity, we used a quantized model variant and turned on prefix caching. Our inference pipeline had a 3–4s median latency in consumer mode, and we needed sub-500ms for a good interactive experience.
[01:34] Evan (SE): Quick interject — just to clarify for listeners: prefix caching here refers to saving the token KV cache for repeated prompt prefixes so we avoid recomputing. That was a big win for their workload.
[01:48] Priya: Right, once we enabled caching plus batching we saw token costs drop pretty drastically. We also reworked how we chunk experimental notes.
[01:58] Maya: Were there any security or compliance hurdles early on?
[02:02] Dr. Anika: Large ones. We operate on patient-adjacent data; even though it's de-identified, our compliance team required customer-managed keys and strict audit logging. Redwood's private and dedicated options, plus KMS integration, were decisive.
[02:19] Sofia: We had a meeting with your security team during the POC — I remember the SOC2 excerpts and the HSM/KMS diagrams chatting back and forth.
[02:28] Liam: The diagrams were helpful, though the initial doc had some typos — it said 'KV cash' in one place which, uh, is obviously 'cache'.
[02:36] (laugh)
[02:39] Evan: Yeah auto-transcripts do that.
[02:41] Maya: So let's talk numbers — Jules, you mentioned latency improvement. What did you measure?
[02:46] Jules: In prototype mode on public endpoints we had 2.8–4.2s median for a single long-form completion in our UI. After onboarding to Redwood Dedicated with tuned batching and a smaller model variant we landed at ~420–480ms median for typical queries. Under burst load (20 concurrent users) p95 was still under 750ms.
[03:08] Priya: And cost per 1k requests dropped by almost 60% once we adjusted batch sizing and enabled prefix caching — that's including infra and token costs.
[03:19] Liam: The savings translated to our business case — we could add more seats without blowing the budget.
[03:25] Maya: That's notable. Did you have to change model prompts or architecture to get those gains?
[03:30] Jules: A bit. We moved to a concise context window, trimmed some system prompt verbosity, and used Redwood's model recommendations. There was a tradeoff — we slightly reduced elaboration sometimes, but overall answer relevance stayed high.
[03:47] Sofia: I remember the A/B we ran — we logged a small change in F1 on our evaluation set but user satisfaction actually improved because of the snappier responses.
[03:57] Dr. Anika: Yeah users prefer a fast helpful answer over a long-winded one that takes four seconds.
[04:03] Maya: Let's touch on integration. Was the SDK/console experience straightforward?
[04:08] Liam: Mostly yes. The SDK had the primitives we needed. We did hit one friction with our infra team: the VPC peering setup had a couple of rounds to get firewall rules right. But Redwood SEs were in the loop and helped.
[04:22] Evan: We logged those issues as tickets and the team pushed a small script to validate peering routes which reduced iteration time.
[04:30] (crosstalk)
[04:33] Maya: Were there any vendor comparisons during your procurement?
[04:36] Dr. Anika: We looked at Anthropic and a managed cloud provider — ManagedCloudAI. The differentiator for us was the combination of Dedicated throughput guarantees and the ops tooling that made rollouts predictable. Also the cost modeling Redwood provided helped quantify savings.
[04:53] Maya: On the topic of customer data: you mentioned KMS. Did you use your own KMS or Redwood-managed?
[04:59] Jules: We used our own KMS via an HSM-backed integration. That gave the security team confidence. Redwood's logging and RBAC model was also critical for audit trails.
[05:11] Sofia: I'll add — Redwood's private mode also allowed you to pin model versions so you control QA rollouts, which I recall was important to you.
[05:19] Liam: Exactly, being able to freeze a model while we validated a change prevented unexpected regressions in the field.
[05:26] Maya: Switching gears — can you share a customer story where the faster inference changed a workflow?
[05:31] Priya: Yes, we had bench users who abandoned the tool when responses were slow. After we improved latency, adoption doubled in one month and time-to-insight dropped by about 40% in our small pilot cohort. That led to more teams requesting access.
[05:47] Dr. Anika: The business impact was clear — we used the adoption numbers to justify a headcount increase for the digital science org.
[05:55] Maya: Nice. For listeners who are technical, what tuning knobs did you lean on most?
[05:59] Jules: Batching policy and KV cache TTLs. Also quantization level on the model variant. We used Redwood's recommended profiles: int8 quant with a slightly larger max tokens limit and a 10s cache TTL for repeated prefixes.
[06:14] Evan: Just to note, the cache TTL varies by workload; for their use case 10s made sense because many queries repeated similar preambles in quick succession.
[06:24] Maya: Any surprises in the POC?
[06:27] Liam: We were surprised by the operational simplicity — we expected more heavy lift. The Redwood console's tracing and per-token breakdown helped us debug a prompt that was causing high token burn.
[06:39] Sofia: Right, that per-token cost breakdown was what lit up the exact offending prompt.
[06:44] Dr. Anika: Also the team was surprised by the human aspect — Redwood's SEs sat with our engineers for a couple sessions and that made the ramp faster than we anticipated.
[06:56] Maya: What about ongoing monitoring and alerts?
[06:58] Jules: We set up a couple of dashboards — latency, p95, token burn — and hooked alerts to PagerDuty for SRE. We also configured quality regression alerts based on prompt-set evals.
[07:11] Priya: We saw one small regression during a model upgrade and the rollback policy kicked in automatically which saved us from a broader issue.
[07:20] Maya: Nice. Listeners often ask about pricing transparency — how did you model cost during procurement?
[07:27] Liam: Redwood provided a spreadsheet with sample batch sizes, expected token counts, and a forecast model. We paired that with our telemetry to produce a 12-month TCO. It was surprisingly accurate.
[07:39] Sofia: We also suggested running a short synthetic benchmark during the POC to validate throughput assumptions — you ran that, right Jules?
[07:45] Jules: Yeah we did a burst test with 100 concurrent simulated users and validated autoscaling behavior. It matched the SLA targets.
[07:55] Maya: Any advice for teams considering a similar move?
[07:58] Dr. Anika: Start with clear success criteria — define latency SLOs, cost per request targets, and privacy controls. Don't treat it as just a model swap; it's an infra and UX project.
[08:10] Liam: Also invest in prompt housekeeping — a lot of gains are low-hanging once you standardize prompts.
[08:16] Maya: Quick lightning round of fun questions before we wrap — favorite debugging tool?
[08:20] Jules: Flame graphs for CPU, but for this work it's the Redwood trace UI.
[08:25] Priya: Logs + sample transcripts.
[08:28] Liam: Coffee.
[08:30] (laughter)
[08:33] Maya: Okay last segment — marketing angle: Anika, what's one quote you'd be comfortable with us using in a case study?
[08:40] Dr. Anika: "Redwood let us move a lab-critical assistant from prototype to production without sacrificing security or speed."
[08:51] Maya: Great — we'll follow up to get exact wording.
[08:54] Sofia: I'll also send over the short metrics summary to include — latency, adoption, and cost delta.
[09:01] Jordan: Producer note: we'll capture that quote, maybe get a voice check.
[09:05] Maya: We're getting close to time — any final thoughts?
[09:08] Jules: For teams worried about complexity, it's worth a short POC. The ops are more predictable than you'd expect.
[09:15] Dr. Anika: I'd echo that — the partnership aspect mattered a lot.
[09:19] Sofia: Thanks for sharing the candid lessons. We'll provide the materials we promised.
[09:23] Maya: Okay we'll do the wrap and next steps — per notes we'll share audio, transcript, case study draft, and the security artifacts.
[09:31] (brief silence)
[09:34] Jordan: Recording stopped.
